title: Dana receives her key
goal: Dana gets her own access key from Alice. She stores it, checks it and reads the memory once, before she uses an agent.
place: Dana's laptop. A terminal in her home directory, `/home/dana`.

steps.title: Alice prepares Dana's access
before: Alice adds Dana to her private registry: one person entry and one member entry in `example-project`.
Then she runs the `provision` command of the registry script. A dry run is the default: the script prints the plan and changes nothing.

frame.title: alice@desk: ~/tenant-pi
frame.source: round 1 of the live proof: the `provision` dry run of the registry script for the test person; the values come from the example registry of the repository

lines.text: 1. create user pi-memory-person-dana (no console access), unless it exists
2. put inline policy agentcore-memory (746 characters), only when it differs
4. create one access key, only when the user has none; write it once into a new key file (mode 0600)
policy characters without white space: 746 of 2048
1. Store the access key in the AWS profile "pi-memory-person-dana" of ~/.aws/credentials (file mode 0600).
2. Save the person config as ~/.config/agentcore-memory/config.json and add "profile": "pi-memory-person-dana".
3. Delete the Bitwarden Send message after the copy. The config file holds no key.
dry run: no AWS call; nothing changed

after: The plan has four steps: the user, the inline policy, the two tags and one access key.
The policy allows two read actions on four namespace trees, and one write action on Dana's proposals only. It has no delete action.
The handoff note fits the config of the dry run, which has no `profile` field. The apply step writes the config file with `profile` already.

steps.title: The coordinator creates the user and the key
before: The coordinator is the agent of the owner with the admin login. After Alice says yes, it runs the same command with `--apply`.

frame.title: coordinator on alice@desk: ~/tenant-pi
frame.source: round 1 of the live proof: the `provision` apply for the test person; the paths and the time are examples

lines.text: created one access key; key file /home/alice/.local/state/agentcore-memory-admin/keys/pi-memory-person-dana-20260302T091512Z.credentials

after: The step creates the IAM user, puts the inline policy, sets the two tags and creates one access key.
It writes the key into a new private file with mode 0600 and never prints the key. Beside it, it writes Dana's person config with the field `profile`.
A second apply changes nothing. Each step runs only when IAM differs from the plan.

steps.title: Dana opens the Bitwarden Send
before: Alice sends Dana a link in a message. She tells Dana the password of the link by voice, not in the message.
The link opens once and expires after one day. Dana opens it and types the password.

frame.title: Bitwarden Send, opened once with the password
frame.source: the key file form and the handoff steps of `packages/agentcore-memory-admin/README.md`, and the config that `provisionApply` writes in `packages/agentcore-memory-admin/src/iam.mjs`; the live proof made no Send

after: The Send holds two texts: the key in the form of the AWS credentials file, and Dana's person config.
Dana copies both now. The link does not open a second time. Then she deletes the message with the link.

steps.title: Dana stores the key in an AWS profile
before: The AWS command line program `aws` stores a key under a profile name. The name must be `pi-memory-person-dana`, because the person config names it.
Dana pastes the two parts of the key when `aws configure` asks for them.

frame.title: dana@laptop: ~
frame.source: the [AWS CLI documentation of `aws configure`](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cli/latest/userguide/cli-configure-files.html); the live proof added the key file to `~/.aws/credentials` instead

after: The key is now in `~/.aws/credentials`, in the section `[pi-memory-person-dana]`. The region goes to `~/.aws/config`.
`chmod 600` lets only Dana read and write the file.

steps.title: Dana checks who she is
before: `aws sts get-caller-identity` asks AWS which identity a key belongs to. It reads no record and needs no right in the policy.

frame.title: dana@laptop: ~
frame.source: the [AWS CLI reference of `get-caller-identity`](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cli/latest/reference/sts/get-caller-identity.html); the live proof ran this check and kept no output

after: The `Arn` ends with `user/pi-memory-person-dana`. The key belongs to Dana's IAM user.

steps.title: Dana reads the global namespace
before: Dana's policy allows a list on `/shared/`. A list reads and changes nothing, so it is a safe first test.

frame.title: dana@laptop: ~
frame.source: the AWS CLI help of `list-memory-records`, and the metadata keys of the live proof (rounds 0 to 2); the live proof printed no AWS CLI list with a record

lines.text: "text": "Every repository of the team runs its tests with `npm test` before a commit."

after: Each record has an id, a text, one namespace and a creation time.

The store adds four metadata keys of its own: `x-amz-agentcore-memory-recordType`, `x-amz-agentcore-memory-strategyType`, `x-amz-agentcore-memory-createdAt` and `x-amz-agentcore-memory-updatedAt`. The glossary calls them the [store keys](#term-store-keys).

steps.title: A read outside her scope fails
before: Dana searches Chen's private namespace with `retrieve-memory-records`. Her policy does not name it.
Then she searches her own proposals namespace. Her policy names it, and she has proposed nothing yet.

frame.title: dana@laptop: ~
frame.source: round 1 of the live proof: the reads of the test person outside and inside its policy

lines.text: aws bedrock-agentcore retrieve-memory-records --memory-id mem-EXAMPLE --namespace /actor/chen/ --search-criteria searchQuery=tests --profile pi-memory-person-dana

aws: [ERROR]: An error occurred (AccessDeniedException) when calling the RetrieveMemoryRecords operation: User: arn:aws:iam::123456789012:user/pi-memory-person-dana is not authorized to perform this operation
aws bedrock-agentcore retrieve-memory-records --memory-id mem-EXAMPLE --namespace /project/example-project/proposals/dana/ --search-criteria searchQuery=tests --profile pi-memory-person-dana

after: IAM checks the namespace of the request against Dana's policy. A read outside it gets an error with the name of her IAM user, and no data.
A read inside her policy can be empty. The answer is then an empty list, not an error.

steps.title: Dana saves the person config
before: Dana saves the config text of the Send as `~/.config/agentcore-memory/config.json`. She adds one optional field, `hostLabel`.

frame.title: ~/.config/agentcore-memory/config.json
frame.source: the fields of `validateConfig` in `packages/agentcore-memory-core/src/index.mjs`; an input file, which no run prints

after: `schemaVersion`: the version of the file form. It is always `1`.
`memoryId`: the id of the one memory of the team. `region`: the AWS region of the memory.
`actorId`: Dana's id. It goes into her namespaces and into the metadata of her proposals.

`projects`: one entry per project. `projectId` is the id, `role` is `member` or `maintainer`, and `remotes` lists the Git remotes of the project. An optional `directories` list maps a directory without a remote.
`profile`: the AWS profile with the key. The file holds no key.
`hostLabel`: a short word for the metadata `host` of a proposal. Without it, the core sends the host name of the computer.
Optional fields with defaults: `topK` (10 records per namespace), `recallTimeoutMs` (3000), `writeTimeoutMs` (10000). A maintainer adds `ledgerPath`.
An unknown field or broken JSON stops the core with the code `config`. So does a missing file that `AGENTCORE_MEMORY_CONFIG_FILE` names. The error never shows a value of the file.

learned: Each person has one IAM user, `pi-memory-person-<actorId>`, with one access key and one inline policy.
The coordinator creates the user and the key with the admin login, after the dry run and Alice's word.
The key travels once, through a Bitwarden Send with a password told by voice.
The key lives in an AWS profile. The person config names the profile and holds no key.
`aws sts get-caller-identity` shows which IAM user a key belongs to.
A read in your own namespaces works, also when it finds nothing. A read in the namespace of another person fails.
cannot: The key cannot be read from the tracker, from a commit or from a log. The scan hooks refuse a commit with a key pattern.
A link without the password opens nothing.
Dana's key cannot read `/actor/chen/` or the proposals of another person. IAM denies the request.
Dana's key cannot create an IAM user or change a policy. Her policy holds no IAM action.
Dana's key cannot delete a record. No person and no maintainer holds a delete action.
